instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 617 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Last spring my cousin Danielle had to decide whether to take a job at a hospital two states away or stay at the clinic where she had worked for four years. She asked her mother first, and her mother told her to stay. If Danielle had stopped there, she would have had an answer, but she would not have had a very good one. She went on to ask three more people, and the decision she finally made was better because of it. Her experience shows why asking several people for advice usually leads to a better choice than asking only one.

The first reason is that every adviser sees only part of the situation. Danielle's mother thought about how far away the new city was and how lonely it might be. Her supervisor at the clinic, who had no reason to want her to leave, admitted that there was no room for promotion where she was and that the hospital would train her in skills the clinic could never offer. A friend who had moved for work a few years earlier talked about costs Danielle had not considered, such as a security deposit, a higher car insurance rate, and the price of flying home for holidays. None of these people was wrong. Each simply knew about a different piece of the problem, and Danielle needed all the pieces before she could see it whole.

A second reason is that people bring their own wishes into the advice they give, often without noticing. Danielle's mother honestly believed staying was the wiser choice, but she also did not want her daughter to live six hours away. One opinion gives you no way to tell where the facts end and the adviser's feelings begin. When you hear from several people, the bias of one tends to show up against the others. Danielle noticed that her mother was the only person who brought up loneliness as the main issue, and that helped her weigh that concern fairly instead of treating it as the whole story.

Third, comparing opinions shows a person where the real question lies. When everyone agrees, that agreement is strong evidence. All four people Danielle asked said the hospital was the better career move, so she could stop worrying about that point. Where they disagreed was on whether the move was worth the personal cost, and that told her exactly what she still had to settle for herself. A patient who gets a second medical opinion works the same way. If two doctors recommend the same surgery, the patient can go ahead with more confidence. If they disagree, the patient knows to ask more questions before agreeing to anything.

Some people argue that too many opinions only cause confusion, and it is true that a person can hide behind endless asking to avoid deciding at all. But the answer is to ask a reasonable number of people who know something about the matter, not to ask just one. Collecting advice is also not the same as obeying it. Danielle did not count votes. She listened, and then she chose for herself, which meant the decision was hers in a way it would not have been if she had simply done what her mother said.

In the end Danielle took the hospital job, but she negotiated a later start date so she could save money for the move, an idea that came from her friend. She has been there eight months and recently began the training her supervisor described. No single conversation would have gotten her to that plan. It took four of them, and that is the best argument I know for asking more than one person.
